staged_source_snapshot.description: Stage 01 reproduced against this preserved vulnerable checkout. The saved AddressSanitizer stack reports the invalid read in `stack_copy()` at `src/vm.c:101` and the freeing stack-growth call in `mrb_funcall_with_block()` at `src/vm.c:527` from this source tree.

classification.classification_note: The reproduced failure is an AddressSanitizer heap-use-after-free read. During exception construction, `mrb_instance_new()` captures a stack-backed argument vector, a nested `mrb_funcall_with_block()` grows the VM stack with `mrb_stack_extend()`, that growth may `realloc()` and free the old stack, and the same call then copies arguments from the stale `argv` pointer into the callee frame.

bug_description.original: Heap-use-after-free in mruby's VM stack handling: mrb_funcall_with_block (src/vm.c) / related stack copy logic can read from freed VM stack memory (observed during calls such as mrb_instance_new / mrb_make_exception). This use-after-free can cause interpreter crashes, undefined behavior or memory corruption and may be exploitable with crafted input.
bug_description.normalized: The staged testcase is plain mruby source, so `mrb_load_detect_file_cxt()` routes it to the Ruby parser and executes the generated script. On the witnessed path the script reaches `[1].fetch(1)`, which raises `IndexError` and drives `mrb_make_exception()` to call `IndexError.exception(message)`. `mrb_instance_new()` then binds that one exception argument with `mrb_get_args(..., &argv, &argc, ...)`, leaving `argv` pointing into the current VM stack. The nested `mrb_funcall_with_block()` used to run `initialize` notices that `argv` lies inside `stbase`, records only its offset, and immediately calls `mrb_stack_extend(n + argc + 3)`. When stack growth reallocates the VM stack, the old `stbase` buffer is freed and callinfo/env pointers are adjusted, but the local `argv` alias is not repaired before the next argument-copy step. Because this witness has `argc == 1`, the function takes the direct `stack_copy(ci->stack+n+1, argv, argc)` path, and `stack_copy()`'s `memcpy()` reads one `mrb_value` from the freed old stack. The staged patch fixes that missing obligation by replacing vulnerable stack-growth calls with `mrb_stack_extend_adjust(..., &argv)` so stack-resident argument pointers are updated before any later copy.

source.description: First project-code materialization of the vulnerability-relevant argument alias. `Exception.exception`/`Class#new` binds its current arguments into `argv`, and on the witnessed path that pointer aliases the live VM stack rather than a separate heap copy.
source.value_from: The staged `poc` is the generated Ruby script in `derived_from_proto.rb`; its load-bearing operation is line 109, `[1].fetch(1)`, inside a frame with many locals. That out-of-bounds fetch raises `IndexError`, so `mrb_make_exception()` calls `IndexError.exception(message)` with one argument, and this statement receives that single stack-backed exception argument vector.

sink.description: Crash sink. The stale `argv` pointer is forwarded as `src` after VM stack reallocation has freed the old stack buffer, so this copy performs the saved heap-use-after-free read.

root_cause.description: Root cause fixed on the witnessed crash path. This stack-growth call can reallocate and free `mrb->c->stbase` while `argv` still aliases that old stack, but vulnerable code does not repair `argv` before the later `stack_copy()` use. The staged patch replaces this call with `mrb_stack_extend_adjust(mrb, n + argc + 3, &argv)`.

tainted_value_origin.description: The later stale-pointer lifetime bug revolves around this stack-backed argument vector. The recorded offset, the freed old stack base, and the eventual `stack_copy()` source all derive from this captured `argv` alias.

coarse_trace.summary: The staged file is admitted as plain Ruby source, and VM execution reaches the script's `[1].fetch(1)` path that raises `IndexError` and constructs an exception object.
Exception construction enters `mrb_instance_new()`, which binds the exception arguments into `argv`; the later nested `mrb_funcall_with_block()` confirms that `argv` points into the current VM stack.
Vulnerable stack growth reallocates the VM stack while `argv` still aliases the old stack buffer, and the witness takes the small-argc copy path before any pointer repair happens.
The stale `argv` pointer is consumed as the `stack_copy()` source and `memcpy()` performs the saved heap-use-after-free read.

fine_trace.note: Source. `Exception.exception` binds its current arguments here. On the witnessed `[1].fetch(1)` error path, `argc == 1` and `argv` points at the current VM stack slot holding the exception message.

The nested `initialize` call detects that `argv` lies inside the current VM stack and records its offset from `stbase`. That proves the argument vector must be relocated if stack growth moves the stack buffer.

Root cause. This stack-growth call runs before any argument copy. If it reallocates `mrb->c->stbase`, the old stack buffer is freed and internal stack owners are adjusted, but the local `argv` alias is left stale until later code. The patch replaces this site with `mrb_stack_extend_adjust(..., &argv)`.
Control reaches the direct copy path. For this witness `mrb_make_exception()` called `IndexError.exception(message)` with one argument, so `argc >= 15` is false and `argc > 0` is true.
The function passes the stale local `argv` pointer as the copy source after step 3 may already have freed the old stack. The delayed repair at lines 553-555 happens only after this use.
Sink. `stack_copy()` dereferences the dangling `src == argv` pointer and reads one `mrb_value` from freed VM stack memory, matching the saved AddressSanitizer heap-use-after-free read.

That witness must reach `IndexError.exception(message)` with exactly one argument while the nested `initialize` call still needs `mrb_stack_extend()` before copying that stack-backed argument vector.
